newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico blue chips end at 7th straight record.
newsitem.headline: Mexico blue chips end at 7th straight record.

text.p: Blue-chip Mexican stocks forged ahead to their seventh consecutive record close on Wednesday as investors sought bargains after an earlier bout of profit-taking.
"We shouted ourselves hoarse today. They began to buy on dips after taking profits and then the hollering started all over again," a floor trader said.
The leading IPC share index closed up 15.35 points, or 0.32 percent, at a record of 4,836.49.

The IPC had reached a record high of 4,869.07 points earlier, fuelled by Tuesday night's drop in domestic interest rates and an extended buying spree in the wake of relatively clean midterm elections Sunday.
Blue chips sagged to a session low of 4,768.70 on what many felt was overdue profit-taking, before bargain-hunters jumped back into the market, dealers said.
"You have efforts at profit-taking, and then you have a set of investors who do not think the end is to hand," said Felix Boni, research head at ING-Barings in Mexico.
"The latter group is getting in on the rise, the strong peso which shows confidence, and trying to catch up with the rest of Latin America," Boni added.
Boni said midsession attempts to take profits were a sign that a "more prolonged correction" could be expected soon.
Bancomer B shares, the most heavily traded of the day, weighed most on the market, and ceded 20 centavos (2.5 cents) to end at 4.50 pesos (57 cents) after a sharp rise Tuesday.
The financial company's A shares gained 2 centavos (less than 1 cent), however, to end at 2.65 pesos (34 cents) after what dealers said was "brisk buying to close the spread with the B class."

Telefonos de Mexico (Telmex), which carries the most weight on the IPC, led the blue-chip trend, and ended up 15 centavos (2 cents) to 20.90 pesos ($2.65), a record in local currency terms. The telecommunications company's American Depository Receipts, meanwhile, shrugged off a sharp fall on Wall Steet to gain 9/16 to 53-5/16, their highest close since the December 1994 peso crash.
The Dow Jones industrial average dropped 119.88 points to end at 7,842.43.
On the broad market, gainers and sliders were evenly balanced, at 54 each out of 127 stocks traded. Trading volume was very heavy at 162.2 million shares.
